You are not bringing them shocking new material.

reflectionWorksheet.label: Medical / Pattern
prompts: Was the blood visible to me, or was it found only on a laboratory test?
If visible, was the urine pink, red, reddish-brown, tea-colored, or another color?
Did I see clots?
Was I able to urinate normally despite the blood?
Did I have flank, back, lower-abdominal, pelvic, or urinary pain?
Did I have burning, frequency, urgency, fever, chills, nausea, or vomiting?
Was there recent significant exercise, trauma, catheterization, cystoscopy, biopsy, or another urinary procedure?
Could menstruation, vaginal bleeding, rectal bleeding, food pigment, medication, hemoglobin, or myoglobin complicate interpretation?
Am I taking anticoagulants, antiplatelet drugs, or another medication relevant to bleeding or urine color?
Have I had urinary infections, kidney stones, prostate problems, kidney disease, or previous hematuria?
If infection was treated, was the urine appropriately rechecked when indicated?
Have microscopy, urine protein, kidney function, imaging, cystoscopy, or other evaluation been performed, and what did each actually show?
Do smoking history, previous pelvic radiation, occupational exposures, cancer history, or family history change my urinary cancer-risk discussion?
Are there proteinuria, elevated blood pressure, edema, reduced kidney function, or other signs that suggest the kidney filters themselves may need attention?

reflectionWorksheet.label: Somatic / Behavioral
prompts: What happens physically in my body when I see red or brown urine?
How often do I inspect the toilet after the original episode?
Do I repeatedly urinate mainly to see whether the color has changed?
Do I repeatedly inspect underwear, tissue, or the toilet because I am afraid blood will return?
Have I started overhydrating, restricting fluids, holding urine, or changing bathroom behavior because of fear?
Have I stopped exercising or having sex because I assume those activities caused the bleeding?
Can I record one meaningful observation without turning the bathroom into a surveillance station?
Which information would actually help a clinician rather than simply feed my anxiety?

reflectionWorksheet.label: Relationship / Functional
prompts: Have I told a partner or trusted person what happened, or am I hiding the symptom because it feels embarrassing?
Has fear of cancer or kidney disease affected my sleep, concentration, work, or relationships?
Am I avoiding intimacy because I fear bleeding or worsening an unknown condition?
Has another person's panic made my own uncertainty harder to manage?
Has another person's dismissal made me question whether the symptom deserves evaluation?
Are cost, transportation, work, insurance, caregiving, or other practical barriers delaying follow-up?
What would make cystoscopy, imaging, laboratory testing, or specialist evaluation feel more manageable?
What support would help me stay engaged with evaluation without making the symptom the center of every conversation?

reflectionWorksheet.label: Childhood / Developmental
prompts: What did I learn growing up about seeing blood?
Did my family respond to physical symptoms with panic, minimization, or practical action?
Was I taught to wait until symptoms became severe before seeking care?
Were urinary, genital, or bathroom problems treated as embarrassing secrets?
Did caregivers model fear of hospitals, tests, needles, scans, or specialists?
Did I grow up hearing that cancer is automatically a death sentence?
Was I taught that talking about urine, menstruation, genital symptoms, or bleeding was inappropriate?
Do I now hide medical symptoms because privacy was confused with silence?
Do I catastrophize because uncertainty was treated as danger in my family?
Which old response pattern would I like to replace with calm medical follow-through?

reflectionWorksheet.label: Ancestral / Generational
prompts: What kidney, urinary, cancer, sickle-cell, stone, or hereditary disease history exists in my biological family?
Are there known inherited kidney disorders or cancer syndromes that matter to my medical history?
How did older relatives respond to bleeding, urinary symptoms, or cancer concerns?
Does my family carry medical mistrust based on previous neglect, discrimination, or poor healthcare experiences?
Which family concerns represent genuine medical risk and which represent inherited fear?
What useful health information do I want future family members to know instead of leaving it hidden?

reflectionWorksheet.label: Philosophical / Symbolic
prompts: What physical facts do I actually know, and what diagnosis has my mind supplied without evidence?
Which parts of the evaluation are within my control today?
Can I treat the image of a red warning light as a prompt to investigate rather than proof the engine is destroyed?
What would accepting uncertainty without ignoring the symptom look like?
If the symptom is a messenger, can I interpret the message simply as "pay attention" rather than inventing what caused it?
What is the next useful action: emergency care, prompt evaluation, repeat testing, follow-up, or stopping unnecessary checking while the medical plan proceeds?

reset.title: See the Signal Once, Then Choose the Medical Step
steps: First identify whether an emergency pattern is present. If you cannot urinate, are passing obstructing clots, have severe flank pain with fever or marked illness, have significant ongoing bleeding with faintness or weakness, or developed blood after major trauma, stop this reset and seek urgent medical care.

If you are medically stable, observe the urine once. Note whether the blood was visible or found only on testing, the general color, whether clots were present, and whether pain or urinary difficulty occurred.
Step away from repeated toilet inspection. Additional bathroom surveillance does not identify whether the source is kidney, ureter, bladder, prostate, urethra, or something outside the urinary tract.
Use a comfortable supported posture and allow breathing to remain easy and natural. Do not hold the breath or use forced breathing as an attempt to stop bleeding.
Name the fact accurately: "I noticed possible blood or abnormal color in my urine. I do not yet know the cause."
Choose the appropriate next medical action: emergency care, prompt medical contact, planned follow-up, repeat testing when advised, or continuing an already-established evaluation.
Do not overhydrate, deliberately dehydrate, hold urine, repeatedly urinate to inspect color, stop prescribed anticoagulants without medical guidance, or use this reset as treatment for the bleeding.
reset.safetyNote: This reset manages the alarm response to seeing blood or abnormal urine color. It does not stop urinary bleeding, treat infection, pass a kidney stone, dissolve clots, treat cancer, repair trauma, or diagnose the source. Do not use calming exercises or symptom tracking to delay urgent care for urinary obstruction, significant bleeding, severe infection symptoms, or major trauma.

critical_alerts: Visible blood or blood clots together with inability to urinate or a painfully distended lower abdomen.
Significant ongoing urinary bleeding accompanied by fainting, marked dizziness, weakness, confusion, pallor, or other signs of substantial blood loss or instability.
Severe flank or back pain together with fever, shaking chills, marked illness, or other symptoms suggesting serious urinary infection with possible obstruction.
Major blunt or penetrating trauma to the abdomen, flank, pelvis, or genital region followed by visible blood in urine or other signs of urinary injury.
Blood at the urethral opening after significant pelvic or genital trauma, particularly when urination is difficult or impossible.
Severe urinary retention, rapidly worsening urinary obstruction, or other inability to pass urine in the context of active bleeding.
seek_immediate_care_if: You cannot urinate and are passing visible blood or blood clots, or you have a painfully distended lower abdomen.
You have significant ongoing urinary bleeding with fainting, marked dizziness, weakness, confusion, pallor, or other signs of substantial blood loss or instability.
You have severe flank or back pain together with fever, shaking chills, marked illness, or other symptoms suggesting serious urinary infection with possible obstruction.
You have major blunt or penetrating trauma to the abdomen, flank, pelvis, or genital region followed by visible blood in urine or other signs of urinary injury.
Blood is present at the urethral opening after significant pelvic or genital trauma, particularly when urination is difficult or impossible.
You have severe urinary retention, rapidly worsening urinary obstruction, or other inability to pass urine in the context of active bleeding.
schedule_care_if: Any new unexplained episode of visible blood in urine, even when it occurs only once or later clears.
Recurrent visible hematuria.
Confirmed microscopic hematuria that persists or recurs according to the clinician's recommended follow-up.
Blood that continues or returns after treatment of an apparent urinary infection.
Painless visible hematuria.
Hematuria in someone with current or previous smoking history or other meaningful urinary-tract cancer risk.
Hematuria associated with abnormal kidney function, proteinuria, high blood pressure, edema, or other possible renal-disease findings.
Recurrent hematuria associated with kidney stones or suspected stone disease.
Hematuria while taking an anticoagulant or antiplatelet medication when the cause has not been adequately established.
Exercise-associated hematuria that persists, recurs, or occurs outside the expected exercise context.
Recurrent unexplained urinary bleeding after previous negative evaluation when new symptoms or clinical risk changes occur.
Urinary bleeding associated with persistent burning, frequency, urgency, pelvic discomfort, or other lower-urinary symptoms.
Relevant personal or family history of urinary cancer, inherited kidney disease, sickle cell disease or trait, or another condition that changes evaluation.
Any hematuria pattern that remains unexplained or is causing substantial functional impairment, anxiety, or repeated healthcare visits without a clear follow-up plan.
medical_safety.self_care_allowed_if: Tracking color, clots, pain, urinary symptoms, and relevant medication context after a single clearly evaluated benign-appearing episode may support follow-up, but these observations are not a substitute for evaluation of visible blood, persistent confirmed microscopic hematuria, recurrent bleeding, clot retention, or other urgent patterns.
medical_safety.do_not_ignore: Blood in urine ranges from benign or temporary causes to serious urinary or kidney disease. Visible blood, persistent confirmed microscopic hematuria, recurrent bleeding, or blood associated with other concerning findings deserves evaluation. Clot retention, significant bleeding with instability, severe infection with possible obstruction, and major urinary trauma require urgent care.
medical_safety.disclaimer: This app is for education and self-reflection only. It does not diagnose, treat, prevent, or cure disease. Seek professional medical care for diagnosis, treatment, medication decisions, or urgent symptoms.
